extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, scientometrics researchers, and peer-review scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Use Bayesian measures to quantify how accurately a journal's peer review process classifies manuscripts (quality vs non-quality) by computing predictive values of acceptance/rejection signals and analysing the effects of acceptance rate, sensitivity, specificity, reviewer/editor quality, and peer-review costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive Value of Acceptance Signal (PVA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The predictive value of an acceptance signal (PVA) tells us how many acceptance signals correspond to quality manuscripts that meet the journal’s publication standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute using Bayes' theorem: PVA = P(X=1 | S=1) = (q * δ1) / (q * δ1 + (1-q) * (1-δ0)). Here q is the prior (acceptance rate / P(X=1)), δ1 is sensitivity (P(S=1 | X=1)) and δ0 is specificity (P(S=0 | X=0)). Use PVA rather than raw editorial decisions to assess how often acceptance signals actually indicate 'quality' according to the journal's standards; the paper warns that a direct interpretation of an editorial decision can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive Value of Rejection Signal (PVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The predictive value of a rejection signal (PVR) tells us how many rejection signals correspond to manuscripts that do not meet the journal’s publication standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute using Bayes' theorem: PVR = P(X=0 | S=0) = ((1-q) * δ0) / (q * (1-δ1) + (1-q) * δ0). Use PVR to quantify how often rejection signals correctly indicate non-quality manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity (δ1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity (denoted δ1) is the probability the review process signals acceptance given a quality manuscript (P(S=1 | X=1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity is a core component of PVA: higher δ1 increases PVA (holding other parameters fixed). The paper models sensitivity as reflecting reviewers' and editors' ability to detect manuscripts that meet the journal's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity (δ0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity (denoted δ0) is the probability the review process signals rejection given a non-quality manuscript (P(S=0 | X=0)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity is a core component of PVR: higher δ0 increases PVR (holding other parameters fixed). It reflects the process's ability to correctly screen out unsuitable manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate (q)
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptance rate q (used as P(X=1) in the model) is the prior probability that a submitted manuscript is of the quality that meets the journal’s publication standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance rate strongly influences PVA and PVR via Bayes' theorem. Low acceptance rates can make PVA low even with good sensitivity/specificity; the authors recommend process changes (e.g., more rigorous desk decisions) to alter the effective prior for externally reviewed submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of acceptance signal vs rejection signal
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'acceptance signal' refers to an affirmative indication from the reviewers that a manuscript is suitable for publication in a given journal. A 'rejection signal' refers to a negative indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signals are the observable outputs (S=1 or S=0) used to compute predictive values; the editor evaluates reviewers' recommendations to produce the signal used in decision-making and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret editorial decisions using Bayes' theorem (avoid direct interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct interpretation of an editorial decision can be misleading; editorial decisions should be interpreted using the predictive values derived from Bayes' theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of reading acceptance/rejection counts naively, calculate P(X|S) (PVA and PVR) using acceptance rate, sensitivity, and specificity to understand the probability that a signal corresponds to true manuscript quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review cost (high / medium / low)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-review cost is modeled (high, medium, low) as a journal-level parameter that affects the behavior and outcomes of the review process in the authors' simulations and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports that highest-impact computer science and world-class open-access mega-journals achieved acceptable PVA and PVR values across high/medium/low costs, while lower-impact journals with high peer-review costs achieved unacceptable predictive values. The authors advise that lower peer-review costs are associated with better reviewer/editor quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer and editor quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of reviewers and editors (implicit in sensitivity/specificity and in the model) affects the accuracy of the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals with better reviewers and editors will have lower peer-review costs and higher PVA/PVR. The paper recommends selecting better editors and reviewers to improve predictive values, particularly for processes handling complex manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous desk decision process (desk screening)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous desk decision process (more stringent editorial triage before external review) is recommended to improve predictive values, especially in journals with low acceptance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend that all submitted manuscripts undergo a rigorous desk decision process to significantly increase the likelihood that manuscripts sent for external review are appropriate, thereby improving PVA and reducing false acceptance/rejection rates for journals with low acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact as a factor in predictive performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal impact influences the peer review predictive values and the economic/profit implications of editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper finds that higher-impact journals (and reputable mega-journals) tend to achieve acceptable PVA/PVR across peer-review cost levels. The authors suggest journals should strive for greater impact, paying attention to profits and losses arising from editorial decision accuracy.
